topics.label: Lecture introduction and scope
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture as an integration of previously introduced immune cells and molecules.

topics.label: Principles of innate recognition through PAMPs, DAMPs and PRRs
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how innate immune recognition distinguishes danger using molecular patterns and appropriately positioned, germline-encoded receptors.

topics.label: Toll-like receptor recognition and signalling
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how toll-like receptors translate microbial recognition into immune responses shaped by their cellular location.

topics.label: Non-TLR recognition pathways and inflammatory activation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how recognition pathways beyond toll-like receptors activate inflammation and can contribute to inflammatory disease.

topics.label: Sentinel-driven inflammation and leukocyte recruitment
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics follow the inflammatory response from sentinel-cell activation to the recruitment of circulating leukocytes into infected tissue.

topics.label: Lymphatic transport and adaptive immune priming
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how drainage from infected tissues enables dendritic cells to initiate adaptive responses in lymph nodes.

topics.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic examines how excessive inflammatory activation becomes a life-threatening systemic response.

topics.label: Mechanisms of inflammation resolution
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic explains how the balance of inflammatory stimulation and inhibition shifts to shut down an immune response.

topics.label: Tissue repair and persistent inflammation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine why inflamed tissue may fail to return to normal, with granuloma formation extending that discussion to protective containment of persistent infection.

topics.label: Lecture close and next lecture
topics.groupedBecause: This closing ends the lecture and identifies complement as the subject of the next lecture.
